rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient covering the full usable organic range at a mid temperature to reveal how many compounds elute, their retention window, and whether compression occurs at either end. A 20 min slope gives enough separation structure without spending too much of the run on an overly shallow first screen.

All 10 compounds eluted with perfect resolution margin, so the main opportunity is reducing analysis time to improve the time term while preserving separation. A moderately steeper full-range gradient should compress the chromatogram and test how much faster we can go before the 6–7 region becomes limiting.

At 14 min the critical 6–7 pair became slightly under-resolved, so move just a bit shallower while keeping the same selectivity conditions. This should recover resolution for the limiting cluster with only a small sacrifice in speed, likely improving CRF further.

The optimum is near 14–16 min, limited by the 6–7 pair, so now probe temperature as a selectivity lever while keeping the faster 14 min gradient. A small drop to 35 C may improve that critical pair enough to retain the short run and surpass the current best CRF.

Lowering temperature worsened selectivity by collapsing the 5–6 pair, so test the opposite direction at the same fast gradient. Raising T to 45 C may shift selectivity in the crowded mid-region enough to improve the limiting pair while keeping the excellent short run time.

Temperature changes hurt selectivity, so keep 40 C and instead slightly reduce the gradient endpoint to make the gradient less aggressive in the late/mid region where the critical cluster elutes. This may open the 5–8 group while keeping total time near the current optimum.

Reducing phi1 from 0.95 to 0.90 improved the critical 6–7 pair and the CRF, so continue that trend with another small decrease in endpoint at otherwise identical conditions. This should further soften the gradient around the crowded elution window and may push the minimum resolution above the apparent scoring threshold while remaining fast.

The best point so far is phi1 0.90, tG 14, where the critical pair is close to the apparent full-resolution threshold; to improve CRF further, the next lever is shortening time while staying near that selectivity optimum. Testing 12 min at the same phi1 and temperature will show whether the time gain outweighs any small loss in the 6–7 separation.

Time is already in the zero-penalty region, so further gains must come from lifting the resolution term to 1.000 at a similarly short run. Because endpoint tuning helped and temperature strongly changes selectivity, test the low-temperature extreme with the current best gradient to see if the crowded 6–7 region opens rather than collapses.

At 25 C selectivity deteriorated badly, and both 35 and 45 C were also worse than 40 C, so the best region remains centered near 40 C; the remaining promising unexplored lever is a modest increase to 50 C with the best gradient to check for a nonmonotonic selectivity improvement. This is a targeted final temperature probe around the current optimum before focusing back on composition/time fine-tuning.

Temperature exploration confirms 40 C is best, so now test whether raising the starting composition slightly alters early-to-mid selectivity enough to relieve the 6–7 bottleneck while keeping the same endpoint and gradient time. Since all compounds already elute quickly, sacrificing a little early retention is acceptable if it improves the crowded central cluster.

Increasing phi0 from 0.05 to 0.10 improved CRF, so continue one more step in the same direction to see if the crowded 6–7 region can be nudged over the effective full-resolution threshold without leaving the zero time-penalty zone. This is a focused local optimization around the current best conditions.

The best result is at phi0 0.10, phi1 0.90, and lowering phi1 previously moved the critical 6–7 pair toward full resolution, so combine the best phi0 with the lower endpoint. This should be a strong candidate to push the minimum resolution above threshold while keeping run time short enough for no time penalty.

Since the optimum is already reached, the best use of a remaining injection is a very local check around the winner; lowering phi1 one more step tests how robust the maximum is to endpoint reduction. This nearby condition should preserve full elution and may confirm the plateau around the optimum without straying far from the best method.

A small rise in phi0 improved performance before, and with phi1 0.85 already giving perfect CRF, this nearby variant tests whether the optimum is a local plateau in starting composition. It should keep the same favorable selectivity pattern while checking robustness on the high-phi0 side.

Two neighboring methods at phi1 0.85 have reached the score ceiling, so probe one more step higher in phi0 to map the extent of the optimum plateau and check whether the faster late elution remains within the zero-penalty region. This stays close to the successful region while exploring its boundary.

Phi0 0.20 with phi1 0.85 pushed the critical pair back below threshold, so test whether restoring the slightly stronger endpoint recovers mid-cluster spacing at this higher starting composition. This maps the upper-phi0 edge of the optimum region while staying near proven zero-penalty conditions.

Since the score ceiling is already achieved, use a remaining injection to define the low-phi0 boundary of the full-CRF plateau by slightly lengthening the already near-threshold phi0 0.05, phi1 0.85 method. A 16 min gradient should improve the 6–7 pair enough to test whether this composition can also reach the maximum.

With the maximum score already found, a useful remaining test is the faster-side boundary of that optimum region. Shortening the winning phi0 0.10, phi1 0.85 method to 12 min checks whether the plateau extends to a steeper gradient or whether the 6–7 pair immediately falls below the full-resolution threshold.

The 12 min version at phi0 0.10 lost just enough 6–7 resolution to drop below the maximum, so test whether the higher-performing phi0 0.15 can better tolerate the steeper gradient. This directly probes whether the optimum plateau extends to shorter tG on the higher-phi0 side.

The global optimum has already been reached, so a remaining informative check is whether the winning composition is robust to a modest temperature increase. This nearby perturbation maps thermal sensitivity around the best method while staying in the most successful composition/time region.

The optimum composition/time has already been found, so use a remaining run to bracket temperature robustness on the low side for the other max-scoring method. This tests whether the 0.15/0.85 optimum is as temperature-sensitive as the 0.10/0.85 case while remaining close to the proven peak region.

With two max-scoring methods already identified, use a remaining run to define the slower-side edge of the optimum at the winning composition. This checks whether the 0.10/0.85 method still stays at the CRF ceiling when the gradient is made slightly shallower, or whether time penalty immediately pulls it below 1.000.

Two max-scoring conditions define the optimum region near phi0 0.10–0.15, phi1 0.85, so a final local boundary test is to lower phi1 at the better of those two starting compositions. This checks whether the full-CRF plateau extends to 0.15/0.80 or whether time penalty appears immediately, while staying close to the established optimum.

This last run probes whether the very near-optimal 0.15/0.80 condition can trade a little of its excess resolution for shorter time and possibly still remain on the score ceiling. It is the most informative remaining local test around the established optimum plateau because 0.15/0.80 at 14 min already has comfortable minR 1.80 with only a small time penalty.
